lesson.title: The Switch: Giving Every Device Its Own Private Lane
lesson.summary: An Ethernet switch is the workhorse of the modern LAN, using MAC addresses to deliver each frame only to the device that needs it instead of sending it to everyone. That selective forwarding is what lets dozens of devices share a network without stepping on each other's traffic.
lesson.body:
An Ethernet switch is a networking device that connects multiple computers, printers, and other equipment into a single local network, and its defining feature is that it does not treat all of those connections the same way. When a frame arrives on one port, the switch looks at the frame's destination MAC address and forwards it out of only the port that leads to that specific device, rather than sending a copy everywhere. This selective, address aware forwarding is what separates a switch from simpler broadcast everything Ethernet hardware, and it is the reason switches form the backbone of essentially every modern wired LAN.

Each port on a switch is its own dedicated, full duplex connection to whatever is plugged into it. A device connected to a switch port has the full bandwidth of that link available in both directions at once, and its traffic does not have to compete with traffic from any other device on a shared cable. This is a fundamentally different arrangement from early Ethernet, which ran over a shared medium where every device's signal occupied the same channel and only one device could successfully transmit at a time. A switch effectively gives every connected device its own private segment.

That combination of dedicated bandwidth and selective forwarding produces two practical benefits. First, scalability: adding a ninth device to an eight port switch by connecting a second switch does not slow down the existing eight, because their traffic was never sharing bandwidth with each other in the first place. Second, a meaningful degree of traffic isolation: a device on port 3 generally never sees the frames destined for the device on port 7, which both reduces unnecessary processing on end devices and makes casual eavesdropping on a switched network considerably harder than it was on old shared medium Ethernet.

Picture a small office with eight computers plugged into an eight port switch. At the same moment, the computer on port 1 sends a print job to a printer on port 5, while the computer on port 3 pulls a large file from a server on port 6. On a shared medium network, these four devices would be contending for the same limited airtime. On the switch, these frames are simply forwarded from port 1 to port 5 and, independently, from port 3 to port 6, and both conversations proceed at full link speed with no interference between them.

How does the switch know that the printer lives behind port 5 and the server behind port 6? It consults an internal forwarding table that maps MAC addresses to ports. Where that table comes from, and what the switch does when it does not yet contain the answer, is a specific and elegant algorithm in its own right, covered in the next chapter on learning switches. For now, the key idea to hold onto is this: the switch's value comes entirely from its ability to look at a destination address and make a targeted forwarding decision, port by port, frame by frame.
